question: On 26 September 2025, the EU Ambassador to Libya1 announced that Operation EUNAVFOR MED IRINI had provided training to 30 maritime officials from both Tripoli and Benghazi. This marks the first time ever that training has been provided to officers from eastern Libya, which is de facto governed by the Libyan National Army (LNA), a non-state entity, not recognised by the EU or the UN.

Moreover, the UN found the LNA to be deeply involved in both war crimes and crimes against humanity. The organisation is connected with the PMC Wagner Group, which is under EU sanctions. Its leader, Khalifa Haftar, has been found liable for war crimes, extrajudicial killings and torture by a US court. In this context: 1.

Which Benghazi-based entities were the final beneficiaries of the training, under what legal basis, agreement or arrangement did this take place, when was this concluded, and can the legal basis, agreement or arrangement be shared with Parliament?
Does the EU consider the LNA to be a legitimate government entity, and if not, why was training provided to such entities exercising state duties?
How is the training compliant with the EU’s obligations under Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union2, and consistent with current sanctions against the PMC Wagner Group?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.1.2026) The final beneficiary of the training provided under Operation Irini was the Libyan Coast Guard (LCG), a unified Libyan institution at operational level, under the umbrella of the Joint Military Committee. 15 out of the 30 trainees were from the Eastern branch of the LCG.

This training was conducted under the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) framework and pursuant to Council Decision (CFSP) 2025/488 of 11 March 20251, which mandates, in Article 4: ‘…EUNAVFOR MED IRINI shall assist the relevant Libyan institutions responsible for law enforcement and for search and rescue at sea, in particular the Libyan Coast Guard and Navy, in the development of their capacities and in their training in law enforcement at sea, in particular to prevent human smuggling and trafficking’.

The EU engages with authorities throughout the country in line with its one Libya policy. The training delivered was focused on damage control and firefighting training, search and rescue and first aid training.

These are standard components of international maritime professional development and are fully compliant with international law, which requires such skills to ensure seafarers can respond effectively to emergencies at sea.
